new_statements.translation: Every syllable in Yi has a tone, but the number of tones varies from place to place, generally 3-5. The Shuangbai speech of the Southern Yi dialect has three tones: high level, mid level and low falling. Besides having tones, some syllables in Yi also carry 'semantic stress' or 'expressive stress'. Stress is the phenomenon in which one syllable among adjacent syllables is pronounced prominently; it occurs in sentences and, in some languages, also within words. E.g. Yunnan Shuangbai Yi do21'lo ve33 'That's it!' / 'Enough!' (a spontaneous exclamation or urgent cry on seeing something abnormal); Liangshan Yi a33'mo33 'Mother!' (a cry of alarm in danger). Onomatopoeic words and interjections of this kind all carry semantic or expressive stress. In addition, semantic stress in Yi serves to distinguish lexical meaning and grammatical meaning.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tone language (Shuangbai Southern Yi: 3 tones, 55/33/21, on every syllable). No positional word-stress rule is given; instead the author recognises a lexically/grammatically contrastive 'semantic stress' (表意重音) and an 'expressive stress' (表情重音) that fall on particular syllables of certain words (interjections, onomatopoeia, and items where stress distinguishes lexical or grammatical meaning). Which syllable bears it is not stated in the portion seen.

new_statements.identity_note: Ache 阿车 (yif, ache1244) is an ethnonym-based ISO split (Bradley/Pelkey 2007) with zero descriptive references in Glottolog. Yunnan (1955:40) reports the Xinping Ache autonym as Nisu (nei33 su33 phɯ21) and their speech as ~93% lexically identical, grammar identical, to local Xinping Yi, i.e. Nisu/Southern Yi; Wang Chengyou (2003) lists 阿车 as an exonym of Nisu; NCPSSD ethnomusicology titles call the Damaidi (Shuangbai) Ache the 'Nisu branch'. The stress statement quoted is from Li Shengfu (1996), whose datapoint is '双柏话/双柏彝语' (Shuangbai Southern Yi) -- Yang (2009:15) files that datapoint as NW Northern Nisu (yiv, nort2718). Li's snippets never use the name 阿车, so the equation Li-1996-Shuangbai = Ache is probable (Shuangbai's Southern-dialect Yi are the Ache plus small Chesu/Shansu groups) but unconfirmed; the statement may equally belong under nort2718. an earlier compilation named source (Lama 2012) does not cover Ache at all: it describes Azhe 阿哲 of Mile (yiz, azhe1235), a different language that Ethnologue confusingly lists as an alternate name of Ache.

sources.note: pp.14-15 (chapter on Southern Yi phonetics): every Yi syllable has a tone; Shuangbai speech has three tones (high level, mid level, low falling); besides tone, some syllables carry 'semantic stress' (表意重音) or 'expressive stress' (表情重音); stress = one syllable among adjacent syllables pronounced prominently, in sentences and in words; examples: Shuangbai Yi do21'lo ve33 'enough!/that's it!', Liangshan Yi a33'mo33 'Mother!'; interjections/onomatopoeia carry it; semantic stress distinguishes lexical and grammatical meaning. No positional word-stress rule in the snippets seen.
